title: Four cells that remember a flash

trials.label: light from the lower right, go signal after 18 dark ticks: the winner fires alone before the go
light from the lower left, go signal after 12 dark ticks: the go sets off the first spike
light from the right (slightly above), go signal after 16 dark ticks: two cells end up firing together

mechanism: Four identical cells sit in a 2x2 block, and each one touches the other three. A cell fires when its voltage reaches 1, and each spike pushes the other three down by 2. When the flash arrives, the cells usually all fire together once, which pushes every one of them far below firing level. While they are held down, the flash keeps shining for three more ticks. The cell on the side the light came from takes in the most light, so it ends up the least far down. That head start is the memory. In the dark, every cell gets the same small steady push, so they climb back together and none overtakes another, though the lead slowly shrinks. Left alone, the leader reaches firing level 10 to 19 ticks into the dark. Its spike pushes the other three down again, and from then on it blinks alone about every 11 ticks. The go signal gives every cell the same extra push. If the leader is already blinking, it just blinks faster. If it has not fired yet, the go signal sets off its first spike. That is always the case at the 4 to 10 tick gaps it was trained on. Near firing level, this push makes every cell climb three times as fast, so in about 1 in 5 test trials the runner-up is close enough behind to cross on the same tick. The two then fire together and stay in step for good. The score rates every spike by how squarely its cell faces the light, so the runner-up's spikes pull it down from 0.87 to 0.68. That is why the overall score is 0.87 rather than the best possible 0.91. It is also why longer gaps of 20 ticks or more score the full 0.91: by then the leader has already fired alone, and a cell that has been pushed down by 2 can never catch up.
evidence:
I re-ran the 4 cells tick by tick with each cell's voltage recorded. The firing matches the repo's own simulator spike for spike. The test set has only 84 possible trials (12 light directions times 7 gap lengths), so I ran every one of them: score 0.871 (the repo's 48-trial test gives 0.873). The best this body can score is 0.911, because a single corner cell can only point diagonally.
- Pairs explain the whole shortfall. In 18 of the 84 test trials, two cells fire together (score 0.68). The other 66 trials all reach the best possible score for their direction (average 0.92). Every pair forms on the first spike, at or after the go signal. Removing the go signal from those 18 trials leaves a single winner every time. Running them on to 200 ticks, all 18 pairs stay locked together, and no third cell ever fires.
- Pairs never form once the leader has fired. It happened in 0 of the 40 trials where the leader fired before the go signal, and in 18 of the 44 where the go signal came first.
- Order of events: at the trained gaps (4 to 10 ticks), the go signal arrives before any spike in the dark in 84 of 84 trials. At the test gaps (12 to 18), the leader fires first in 40 of 84. Left alone, the leader first fires 10 to 19 dark ticks after the flash, depending on direction.
- The lead shrinks but the order holds. In the dark, the gap between the top two cells shrinks by exactly 1/16 every tick, so it halves about every 11 ticks. For light from the upper right it is 0.61, 0.44, 0.32 and 0.23 at ticks 3, 8, 13 and 18.
- The training directions hid the problem. On the 12 training directions, pairs form only when light comes straight from one side. Then two cells are exactly tied, and a pair scores the same as one cell (0.71). The test directions sit halfway between, where the runner-up is close but not tied. All 18 test pairs come from directions 15 degrees off a side.
- Length of the dark gap (all 12 test directions): 0.60 with no gap (4 of 12 trials silent), 0.88 at 4 to 12 ticks, 0.85 at 14 and 16, 0.88 at 18 and 19, and 0.911 (the maximum, no pairs) for every gap from 20 to 100 ticks.
- No go signal at all: between ticks 40 and 200, exactly one cell fires, every 11 ticks. It is the cell facing the light in 12 of 12 directions. With the go signal on, it fires every 5 ticks.
- Messages off: 0.00. With messages off, all four cells fire on the last flash tick and reset to zero, so afterwards they always fire together, and firing on every side at once points nowhere.
- Strength of the push-down, 0 / -0.5 / -1 / -1.25 / -1.5 / -2 (evolved) / -3: 0.00 / -0.14 / 0.27 / 0.85 / 0.91 / 0.87 / 0.80.
- Messages on only during the flash: 0.00. Only after the flash: 0.00. So the push-down does two jobs: it holds the cells down while the light is written in, and it keeps the winner alone afterwards.
- Leak (how fast voltage drains away), 1/32, 1/16 (evolved), 1/8, 1/4: 0.89, 0.87, 0.56, then 0.00 with every trial silent. If the steady push is doubled along with the leak, the score holds: 0.88 at 1/8 and 0.85 at 1/4. With leak 1/8 and the evolved push, the cells settle exactly at firing level and stop blinking on their own, and the memory fades: 0.79 at a 10-tick gap, 0.42 at 18, and 0.00 from 24 on.
- Flash length 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 ticks: 0.08 / 0.38 / 0.66 / 0.87.
